items.passage: # Rolling back a failed release **Applies to:** Container Service, Functions ## Symptoms - A release has introduced errors and must be reverted - The previous revision is needed while a fix is prepared ## Common causes - A defect reached production that testing did not catch - A configuration change had unintended effects ## Resolution

items.title: Rolling back a failed release
items.passage: ## Resolution 1. Open the revisions page for the service and identify the last revision that was healthy. 2. Select roll back on that revision. Traffic moves within roughly thirty seconds and no rebuild takes place. 3. If the release included a database migration, roll the migration back before the service, or the older code will encounter a schema it does not expect. 4. Record the incident and the reason for the rollback before deploying a fix, while the detail is still fresh. ## Notes Rollback restores the container image and its configuration together. It does not restore data.

items.title: Build failures caused by dependency resolution
items.passage: ## Resolution 1. Pin your dependencies with exact versions and commit the lock file. Unpinned dependencies are the cause in the large majority of cases of this kind. 2. Compare the runtime version declared in your build configuration against the version you use locally. 3. Clear the build cache from the settings page and trigger a fresh build to rule out a corrupted artefact. 4. If a specific dependency is failing to resolve, check whether its registry is reachable from the build network. ## Notes Build logs retain the full resolution output for thirty days, which is usually enough to identify which version changed.

items.title: Responding to a suspected account compromise

items.title: Webhook delivery, retries and signature verification
items.passage: ## Resolution 1. Check the webhook delivery log, which records every attempt with the response status and body for the last seven days. 2. Return 2xx as quickly as possible and process the event asynchronously. Deliveries time out after five seconds. 3. Compute the signature over the raw request body before any parsing. Re-serialising JSON changes the bytes and invalidates the signature. 4. Make your handler idempotent using the event identifier. At-least-once delivery means duplicates are expected rather than exceptional. ## Notes Failed deliveries are retried with backoff for twenty-four hours, after which the endpoint is disabled and the account is notified.

items.title: Backups, retention and point-in-time restore
items.passage: ## Resolution 1. Identify the point you need to restore to. Point-in-time recovery covers any moment within the retention window rather than only backup times. 2. Restore into a new database instance rather than over the existing one, so the current state is preserved while you verify the restore. 3. Allow roughly ten minutes per hundred gigabytes for the restore, and considerably longer where the instance is also under load. 4. Verify the restored data before switching traffic, and keep the original instance until that verification is complete. ## Notes Retention is seven days on Standard, thirty days on Business and ninety days on Enterprise plans.

result.answer:
Hi,

For very large extracts, the recommended approach is to use the export endpoint, which runs asynchronously and returns a download link [DOC-API-002]. This avoids the need to iterate through pages manually, which can be slow and prone to issues if the data changes during iteration [DOC-API-002].

If you must use pagination for other reasons, please note the following:
1. Use cursor pagination rather than offset pagination to prevent skipping or repeating records when items are inserted mid-iteration [DOC-API-002].
2. Keep the page size at or below 200, as larger requests are rejected rather than truncated [DOC-API-002].
3. Pass the `next_cursor` value from each response as the `cursor` parameter for the next request, and stop when it is null [DOC-API-002].
4. Be aware that cursors expire after one hour, so long-running iterations should handle expiry by restarting from a recorded checkpoint [DOC-API-002].

Regarding the export endpoint, jobs covering more than a million records commonly take several minutes to process [DOC-DATA-001]. Download links are valid for 24 hours, but the underlying file is retained for seven days, so you can request a fresh link if the original expires [DOC-DATA-001]. Note that the export reflects the snapshot taken when the job started, so records created during processing are not included [DOC-DATA-001].

Let us know if you need further assistance.

Best regards,
Support Team
result.answer_reason: The documentation provides clear guidance on using the export endpoint for large extracts and specific rules for cursor pagination, including page size limits and cursor expiration, which directly address the user's issues with rejected large page sizes and slow iteration.

issue_from_ticket.body: Our spend cap stopped a production workload overnight. We need it raised immediately and then we need to reconsider how we have this configured.

items.title: Usage limits, overage and spend controls
items.passage: ## Resolution 1. Check the current period usage against the plan allowance on the billing page. 2. Decide deliberately between a hard spend cap, which stops the service, and overage, which continues at the listed rate. Production workloads generally need the second. 3. Configure alerts at fifty, eighty and ninety-five per cent of allowance rather than relying on the cap as a warning. 4. Where a cap has stopped a production service, an account owner can raise it immediately from the billing page and service resumes within a minute. ## Notes Spend caps apply per organisation and cannot currently be set per project.

items.title: Usage limits, overage and spend controls
items.passage: # Usage limits, overage and spend controls **Applies to:** All plans ## Symptoms - Service was throttled after a traffic increase - Overage charges appeared unexpectedly - A spend cap stopped a production workload ## Common causes - Plan allowance was consumed before the end of the period - A spend cap was configured and reached - Overage protection is disabled, so usage continued beyond the allowance ## Resolution

items.title: Changing plans, and how proration is calculated
items.passage: ## Resolution 1. Upgrades take effect immediately and are prorated for the days remaining in the period. The invoice shows the calculation as a separate line. 2. Downgrades take effect at the start of the next period so that paid-for capacity is not lost. The scheduled change appears on the subscription page. 3. Credits from a downgrade or an adjustment are applied against the next invoice by default rather than refunded to the payment method. 4. Where a refund rather than a credit is required, an account owner should raise the request within thirty days of the invoice. ## Notes Annual plans cannot be downgraded mid-term, but capacity can be reduced with effect from the renewal date.

items.title: Understanding API rate limits and quota tiers
items.passage: ## Resolution 1. Read the rate limit headers returned with every response. They give the limit, the remaining allowance and the reset time, which is more reliable than inferring the limit from behaviour. 2. Confirm whether the endpoint has a specific limit. Search and export endpoints are more expensive and are limited more tightly than reads. 3. Implement exponential backoff with jitter on 429 responses rather than retrying immediately, which prolongs the throttling. 4. Where sustained higher throughput is genuinely required, the limit can be raised on Business and Enterprise plans through an account request. ## Notes Limits are enforced per organisation. Issuing more keys does not increase the available quota.

items.title: Understanding your invoice and usage breakdown
items.passage: ## Resolution 1. Open the usage breakdown for the period, which itemises charges by service and by environment. 2. Look for resources in staging or development environments, which are billed at the same rate as production. 3. Check the billing period dates at the top of the invoice. The period runs from the anniversary of the subscription date. 4. Set a usage alert on the billing page so that unexpected accrual is noticed during the period rather than at the end of it. ## Notes Invoices are finalised three days after the period ends. Adjustments requested before finalisation appear on the same invoice.

items.title: Container deployments failing during the health check phase
items.passage: ## Resolution 1. Confirm the container is listening on the port declared in the service definition. A mismatch here produces a health check failure that looks like a timeout. 2. Increase the initial delay if the application needs time to warm up before it can answer. Thirty seconds is a reasonable starting point for services that load models or caches. 3. Compare the environment variables present in the deployment against those the application requires. Missing configuration frequently causes a silent startup failure. 4. Inspect the container logs from the failed revision rather than the running one; the rollback replaces the logs shown by default. ## Notes

items.title: First deployment: a walkthrough
items.passage: # First deployment: a walkthrough **Applies to:** All plans ## Symptoms - A new user does not know where to begin - The first deployment fails for unclear reasons ## Common causes - Required configuration has not been set - The project structure does not match what the build expects ## Resolution 1. Create a project, then a service within it. Resources belong to services and services belong to projects. 2. Connect a repository or push a container image. The build service detects common project layouts automatically. 3. Set any environment variables the application needs before the first deployment rather than after it. 4. Deploy, then watch the logs for the first sixty seconds. Most first-deployment problems are visible immediately in startup output. ## Notes

items.passage: # Build failures caused by dependency resolution **Applies to:** Build Service ## Symptoms - Builds that previously succeeded now fail without code changes - The build works locally but fails in the pipeline - Dependency resolution takes far longer than usual ## Common causes - An unpinned dependency released a new incompatible version - The build environment uses a different language runtime than the local machine - The dependency cache holds a partially written artefact ## Resolution

result.answer:
Hi there,

For connecting your CI pipeline, the recommended approach is to create a service account rather than using a personal key [DOC-INT-001]. This ensures that access survives staff changes, as keys issued to individual users are removed when that user is deleted [DOC-AUTH-004].

To set this up securely:
1. Grant the service account only the specific projects and permissions the pipeline needs, and review these grants whenever the pipeline changes [DOC-INT-001].
2. Store the credential as an encrypted secret in your pipeline provider; never store it in the repository [DOC-INT-001].
3. Test the pipeline credential separately from the deployment logic to distinguish authentication failures from deployment issues [DOC-INT-001].
4. Since service account keys do not expire by default, set an expiry and rotate them on a schedule [DOC-INT-001].

Let us know if you need further assistance with the setup.
